notes.meaning: The Sadducees were a Jewish group who said there is no life after death. They start by quoting a law of Moses from Deuteronomy 25. If a man died with no children, his brother was to marry the widow, and their first child would count as the dead man's. This kept his family name and his land from dying out.

They tell a story of seven brothers who each marry the same woman and die childless, and then she dies too. It may not have really happened. It seems to be an old puzzle they liked to use against people who believed in the resurrection, and they may have made the number big on purpose. Matthew Henry notes a quiet lesson here: those who outlive others still die in the end.

Here is the trap: whose wife will she be when the dead rise? The Sadducees assumed that life after the resurrection must be just like life now, with the same marriages. If so, the idea looks silly, and they hoped to prove there is no resurrection at all. Some Jewish teachers of the time did picture heaven in very earthly ways, which made the puzzle seem stronger.

Jesus names two reasons for their mistake. They did not truly know the Scriptures, which teach that the dead will rise. And they did not know God's power, which is fully able to raise the dead. Calvin says the resurrection is beyond what our senses can grasp, so we believe it only when we think about God's endless power alongside his Word.

Resurrection life is not just this life carried on. People will not marry, because they will be like the angels: they will never die, so there is no need for new births. This does not mean they will have no bodies. It means they will be free from the weakness and needs of this life, and no one will be left out or jealous.

Jesus proves the resurrection from the books of Moses, the part of Scripture the Sadducees valued most. God spoke these words at the burning bush long after Abraham, Isaac and Jacob had died, yet he said "I am" their God, not "I was." God is the God of living people, so these men must still be alive with him. If their souls live on, their bodies will one day be raised as well. Jesus also says God spoke this "to you," because Scripture speaks to each reader.

The crowds were amazed at how clear and solid his answer was. Matthew Henry thinks it was new to them because their teachers had explained Scripture so poorly. Adam Clarke notes that truth often shines brighter when it is opposed.

Jesus had "muzzled" the Sadducees. The Pharisees were a strict religious group who did believe in the resurrection. They may have been glad their rivals were beaten, but they still gathered to find a new way to catch Jesus. Matthew Henry says they were more upset that Jesus was honored than pleased that the truth was defended.

An "expert in the law" was not a courtroom lawyer. He was a scholar of the law of Moses, also called a scribe. He came to test Jesus. Older commentators differ on his motive. Wesley and Barnes think he meant no real harm, since Mark says Jesus told him he was not far from God's kingdom. Calvin sees the question as a trap.

Teachers of the time argued about which command mattered most. Some said sacrifice, some circumcision, some the Sabbath. They counted 613 commands in the law. If Jesus picked just one, they could accuse him of slighting the rest.

Jesus quotes Deuteronomy 6:5. We are to love God with everything we are: heart, soul and mind. That means loving him more than anything else and giving him all our powers. This is the first and greatest command because all true obedience flows from it. Calvin notes that God asks for love, not forced service, because he wants worship that is freely given.

The second command comes from Leviticus 19:18. It is "like" the first because it grows out of loving God, and real love for others shows that we love God. Loving your neighbor "as yourself" means caring for others as truly as you care for your own good. We treat them the way we would want to be treated. Calvin says this corrects our habit of thinking only of ourselves.

Everything the Law and the Prophets teach about how to live hangs on these two commands, like links of a chain hanging from the first and last. Love sums up all that God asks of us. Calvin adds that Jesus is speaking about commands, not about the whole Bible. God's free forgiveness of sins is a gift we receive, not something we earn by keeping these commands.

Now Jesus asks the questions. "The Christ" means the Messiah, the promised King God would send. Jesus asks whose descendant he would be. The Pharisees answer easily: David's, as the prophets had promised. Matthew Henry adds that each of us should ask ourselves the same question: what do we think of Christ?

"In the Spirit" means David wrote by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, as a prophet. So when David calls the Messiah "Lord," it carries God's authority. Calvin says Jesus stresses this to show the psalm is not about David's own reign but about the future reign of Christ.

Jesus quotes Psalm 110:1: God said to David's Lord, the Messiah, "Sit at My right hand." To sit at a king's right hand meant the highest honor and power. Spurgeon adds that sitting pictures rest after his work is finished. He reigns until every enemy is placed under his feet, like a footstool. Calvin says believers can take comfort that no one can overthrow his kingdom.

A father does not normally call his descendant "Lord." The only answer is that the Messiah is both God and man. As God, he is David's Lord. As man, he is David's son. Jesus later calls himself "the root and the offspring of David" in Revelation 22:16.

No one could answer, and from then on no one dared try to trap him with questions. Matthew Henry notes that many people are silenced by the truth without being changed by it. Adam Clarke observes that his enemies now stopped asking questions and began planning how to kill him.
